claims.text: In high-entropy alloys outside Nb-Ta and titanium-rich systems, superconducting behavior is governed by the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The degree of chemical disorder influences the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The presence of elements with high electron-phonon coupling constants influences the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys broadens electronic states.
Chemical disorder combined with elements having high electron-phonon coupling can enhance the density of states at the Fermi level.
An enhanced density of states at the Fermi level promotes superconductivity.
Substitution with elements having higher electron-phonon coupling constants will increase the superconducting critical temperature.
Substitution with elements having lower electron-phonon coupling constants will decrease the superconducting critical temperature.
Systematic elemental substitutions are expected to produce corresponding changes in the density of states at the Fermi level.
The proposed relationship applies to single-phase high-entropy-alloy solid solutions with random atomic distributions.
The proposed relationship does not cover alloys with significant phase separation or ordered structures.
The interaction between chemical disorder and electron-phonon coupling in controlling the Fermi-level density of states in uncharacterized high-entropy alloys is not well established.
